sets.title: Borrowing a rain gauge
sets.transcript:
M: Hi, come on in. You're the one who emailed about borrowing a rain gauge?
W: Yes, that's me. It's for my science fair project. I want to measure how much rain falls at school every day for five weeks.
M: Five weeks, okay. We've got two gauges in the cupboard, and the plastic one's easier to read. Where were you planning to put it?
W: I thought about the roof first, because nothing's in the way up there.
M: Students can't go on the roof, I'm afraid. It's a safety rule. But here's an idea. Put it on the ledge outside this window. You could check it without even going outside.
W: That would be easy. But I read that a gauge shouldn't sit right next to a wall. The building would block some of the rain, especially when it's windy.
M: Hmm, that's true. And this window faces away from most of our storms. So where else?
W: The vegetable garden behind the gym. It's open, there aren't any trees near it, and there's an old fence post in the corner I could tie it to.
M: The garden? I'm worried about the sprinklers. If they spray the gauge even once, your number for that day is useless.
W: I asked the garden club yesterday. They stopped using the sprinklers last month. Now they water by hand, and they said they'll stay away from that corner.
M: Well, you've really done your homework. All right, the garden it is. How often will you read it?
W: Every morning at about a quarter to eight, before the first bell. I'll write the number in my notebook and then empty it.
M: Good. And if there's a freezing night, bring it inside, because ice can crack the plastic.
W: Got it. Can I take it today?
M: Sure. Just sign this form, and bring it back to me when your five weeks are over.

sets.title: How sea stacks form
sets.transcript:
So today we're going to follow a piece of coastline through a very slow change. You've probably seen pictures of tall columns of rock standing in the sea, a little way out from a cliff. Geologists call these sea stacks, and I want to walk you through how one forms, step by step, because it doesn't happen all at once.

It starts with a headland. That's a piece of land that sticks out into the sea, with water on three sides. Because it sticks out, waves hit it from more than one direction, so it takes more of a beating than the bays on either side. Now, no rock is perfectly solid. Even hard rock has cracks running through it, and the cracks are where the sea gets to work.

Here's the first step. When a wave slams into a crack, it traps the air inside and squeezes it. Think of pushing down on a bicycle pump with your finger over the end. You can feel the air pushing back. In the rock, that squeezed air presses outward on the walls of the crack. Then the wave pulls back, the air suddenly expands, and the rock around it is shaken loose a little. Repeat that thousands of times a day, and a crack slowly becomes a gap. At the same time, waves throw sand and pebbles against the cliff, which grinds it away like sandpaper.

Step two. Over many years, the gaps widen into caves. And because the headland is hit from both sides, you often get a cave on each side, growing toward each other. When they finally meet in the middle, you've got an arch, a bridge of rock with the sea running underneath.

Step three. The arch doesn't last. Waves keep cutting at its base, while rain, wind and frost attack the top. Eventually the roof of the arch gets too thin to hold its own weight, and it falls. That's usually sudden, often during a storm. What's left standing on the seaward side, cut off from the land, is the stack.

And the story keeps going. The waves now attack the stack from every side, mostly at the bottom, where they hit hardest. It gets thinner at the base until one day it topples too. What remains is a short stump, which may only show at low tide.

How do we know the stages really come in this order? I'm confident they do, and here's why. First, along one coast you can often see every stage side by side: a headland with caves, an arch further along, then stacks and stumps. Second, we have old photographs. At a place called Harrock, a photograph from about a hundred years ago shows an arch. Today, in that same spot, there's no arch, just a single stack standing alone in the water.

So next time you see a sea stack, remember that you're looking at what's left of a headland, and that the next stage has already begun.
